title: The ghost and the curly tail
hook: a ghost, a dog's curly tail, and why seva still matters when the world won't change
carry: seva: serving others changes the one who serves
tomorrow: a mongoose, half gold, says a king's great sacrifice isn't enough. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna picked up his bow. With your own work, worship; offered work is careful work.

A year of volunteering, donating, showing up for the cause, and the problem looks exactly the same. The shelter is still full. The inbox is still full. And a quiet voice asks: what's the point? Vivekananda took that question seriously. In his Karma Yoga lectures he answered it with a strange little story about a man, a ghost, and a dog's tail that would not stay straight. The chapter's title sounds almost rude: We Help Ourselves, Not the World.
screen: `THE PROBLEM LOOKS THE SAME.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Vivekananda tells it. A man wanted a ghost to do his work for him, and he got one. But there was a catch: the ghost had to be kept busy every minute, or it would kill him. It finished every job in no time. Build a house: done. Clear a field: done. The man, terrified, ran to a wise teacher, who said: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail. The ghost pulled the tail straight. Let go, and it curled back up. Pulled again. Curled. That kept it busy. The world, Vivekananda said, is like that dog's tail. People keep pulling it straight; let go, and it curls. So is helping pointless? No. That's the turn. When we help, he said, we're not fixing the world. The world will go on. We are the ones being changed. So, he said, be grateful to the person you help: they gave you the chance. Hindus call this kind of help seva, selfless service, and many temples run on it. And serve, he said, like a master, not a slave, the way Janaka ruled. The Gita has a picture for it: the one who acts, offering the action and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by it, the way a lotus leaf sits in water and stays dry. The tail still curls. You keep straightening it anyway, and you stay dry.
screen: `A GHOST THAT MUST BE KEPT BUSY.` · `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.` · `SEVA: THE HELPER IS THE ONE WHO CHANGES.` · `A LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `SEVA CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back: a cause, a messy house, a relative who won't change. Breathe in and feel how much you want the result; breathe out and set the result down beside you, just for now. Then picture doing the next small piece anyway, because it's worth doing, like the lotus leaf: in the water, and dry.
Master, one who works freely, not for reward. In seva, we help ourselves, not the world: the work changes the worker. Stay dry like the lotus leaf.
Your line: seva: serving others changes the one who serves. The tail still curls, and the helper still grows. Day two hundred sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: In seva, service offered freely, many Hindus aim to help without clinging to results or credit, often using the Gita's image of the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet.

fork.reveal: the world is a curly tail, and the helper is the one who grows. so be grateful to the ones you serve.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 5.10: 'like a lotus leaf by water' — untouched by what it sits in.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga is about fixing the world through good works.
what it means: the work is worth doing, but its deepest effect is on the one who does it, freely and without clinging.

what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's 'we help ourselves, not the world' reframes service as spiritual discipline; the lotus-leaf image is Gita 5.10 (padmapatram ivāmbhasā), a common picture in Indian texts for being in the world without being stained by it.

a boss who has others do the work for him

a sacred fig tree, pictured upside down
